heading: The Americans and their families paying the price

cases.name: The Ali family
cases.title: Same interview, same day. Only half the family made it home.
cases.detail: Wael Ali's wife and three children were all told their visas were approved at a single January 20 interview, but only the two sons' visas were issued before the pause took effect the next day. Ten months later, their mother and 16-year-old sister are still in Egypt, refused again in October on public-charge grounds.

cases.name: The Linares family
cases.title: Her first six weeks were in intensive care. Her father was barred from her side.
cases.detail: Freddy Linares flew to Guatemala for his visa interview while his U.S. citizen wife, Yessica, was eight months pregnant, and the 75-country ban stopped him from coming home. Their newborn daughter went through surgery and six weeks of neonatal intensive care without him, and by November he still had not met her.

cases.name: The Rami–Laasri family
cases.title: His daughter is an American citizen. He has never held her.
cases.detail: Hanan Rami gave birth in Delaware on August 28, weeks after a consular officer in Casablanca told her husband, Youness Laasri, that his visa would have been approved if not for the ban. The ban has since been struck down and the couple asked for expedited processing, but he is still waiting in Morocco.

cases.name: The Mitchell–Baugh family
cases.title: He's 92 and depends on his wife for care. She's stuck in Jamaica.
cases.detail: Carol Marie Baugh, 71, is the caregiver for her 92-year-old husband in Florida, who has multiple medical conditions, but she has been stranded abroad since traveling for her visa interview. Even after the ban was overturned, Kingston refused her visa again in October, and their son has had to take over his father's care.

cases.name: The Temaj–Wilbanks family
cases.title: She left for a short trip to her visa interview. Her children started school without her.
cases.detail: In May 2026, Lorenza Temaj Jiguan left her husband and two children in Maryland for what should have been a routine immigrant visa interview in Guatemala. The trip turned into six months stranded abroad, and her children began a new school year without their mother.

cases.name: A Florida family
cases.title: She lost her pregnancy alone. A visa pause kept her husband away.
cases.detail: A U.S. citizen in Florida told a federal court that she suffered a miscarriage without her husband by her side, because his immigrant visa was caught in the 75-country pause.

source.label: Storie v. Trump · District court opinion · Aug 25, 2026 · citing ECF No. 7-4 at 23–24

cases.name: Dr. Fernando Lizcano Losada
cases.title: The government called him "extraordinary." Then it shut the door.
cases.detail: In January 2025, USCIS approved the Colombian endocrinologist's EB-1A petition, a category reserved for people of extraordinary ability whose work will benefit the United States. A year later his visa was refused under the 75-country pause, and in late October 2026 he was still in Bogotá, waiting to bring his biomedical research to the United States.

cases.name: Fahimeh Mohajeri and Miad Ghaffari Ajrabadi
cases.title: Two years after her interview and still without an answer. A federal judge called the wait reasonable.
cases.detail: Fahimeh Mohajeri, the wife of a U.S. citizen, was interviewed in Yerevan in April 2024 and then left in "administrative processing" with no decision. Twenty-six months later, a federal judge dismissed the couple's lawsuit to compel an answer, ruling that the wait did not count as unreasonable delay.

source.label: Ghaffari Ajrabadi v. Rubio · District court opinion · Jun 18, 2026

cases.name: The Tonelli family
cases.title: The email said "final interview." The same day, the door slammed shut.
cases.detail: Music professor Mark Tonelli married Luciana in 2024 and filed a petition for her and his stepson to join him from Brazil about a week after the wedding. More than a year later, the couple got word they qualified for their final interview, the last step in the process. That same day, the State Department froze immigrant visas for 75 countries, Brazil among them. "It's been agonizing every day," Tonelli told the Chicago Sun-Times in April 2026.
